slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by separating the theorem from the picture students usually remember. The point is not merely that triangles are convenient in the plane; it is that affine dimension bounds the number of witnesses needed for every convex representation. The deck will make the reduction step visible rather than treating the theorem as a static statement.

slides.title: Theorem Statement
slides.notes: State the theorem in the coefficient language because that is the form students will inspect in computations. Stress the affine-dimension refinement immediately. If a set lies in a plane inside a much larger space, the representation count follows the plane, not the surrounding coordinate system.

slides.title: Affine Dimension
slides.notes: Make the dimension count tactile. Pick an anchor point and draw the difference vectors. The theorem is controlled by how many independent directions these differences span. This is why a planar polygon embedded in three-dimensional space still needs at most three points, not four, to represent a point in its convex hull.

slides.title: Reduction Move
slides.notes: Explain the proof as an algorithm rather than a contradiction. If more than dimension plus one points appear, their differences are affinely dependent. Moving the coefficient vector along that dependence preserves the represented point and the total weight, while the step size is chosen so that one coefficient reaches zero without making any coefficient negative.

slides.title: Planar Hull
slides.notes: Use the planar picture to match the notebook target. The full hull may involve many sample points, but the representation of one point can be certified by a single triangle. This does not mean the triangle equals the hull; it only needs to contain the particular point being represented.

slides.title: Barycentric Coefficients
slides.notes: Focus on the coefficients as the object to audit. A visual triangle is persuasive, but the certificate is the vector lambda. It must reconstruct the point, sum to one, and have no negative entries. Zero entries should be celebrated because they reveal a lower-dimensional face representation.

slides.title: Conic Variant
slides.notes: Introduce the conic form as the sibling theorem. Removing the normalization equation changes the count and the algebra, but the proof instinct is the same: too many rays create a linear dependence, and moving along that dependence preserves the represented vector while eliminating a redundant coefficient.

slides.title: Simplex Support
slides.notes: Clarify that the theorem gives an upper bound on witness size. A point on an edge in the plane needs only two vertices, even though the theorem allows three. Once students watch zero coefficients identify faces, they can read the geometry and the algebra as the same certificate.

slides.title: Reduction Algorithm
slides.notes: Convert the proof into a checklist students can execute by hand or in code. The important invariants are simple: the represented point is unchanged, coefficient sum remains one, and nonnegativity is preserved by the chosen step. Repeating the move must eventually stop because at least one active coefficient disappears each time.

slides.title: Boundary Cases
slides.notes: Use boundary cases to prevent overreading the theorem. Caratheodory gives a maximum number of witnesses, but the geometry may be cheaper. Interior, edge, and vertex positions correspond exactly to three, two, and one positive coefficient in a planar simplex, so the coefficient vector reveals the face structure.

slides.title: Numerical Checker
slides.notes: Tie this slide directly to the notebook checks. A Caratheodory certificate is easy to audit because it has three visible tests: equality, normalization, and nonnegativity. The computation is not the proof, but it disciplines the diagram by requiring the displayed small witness to reconstruct the point numerically.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Frame the lab as a way to test the theorem's inputs. Moving the target point changes which face is active. Adding extra samples changes the hull but not necessarily the witness count. Embedding the same data in a larger coordinate space checks whether students are using affine dimension rather than ambient dimension.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by naming the durable idea: convex membership has short certificates in finite dimension. The theorem justifies replacing a large cloud of possible witnesses by a simplex-sized list. The next section on extreme points and faces will use this compression mindset to identify which witnesses are structurally essential.
